name: Kim Gordon
who_line: Anti-fashion as a habit, not a pose. She dresses against the generic thing that makes you feel safe.
who: Kim Gordon is the bassist and voice of Sonic Youth, and later a solo artist, writer, and the co-founder of X-Girl. Anti-fashion is a habit, not a pose. The X-Girl clothes were what she and Daisy von Furth already hunted in thrift stores — fitted, clean, a little preppy — because oversized skate menswear did not fit a woman’s body.
She is wary of being sold as a feminist icon. To Numéro (2024): she does not like how feminism is now used as branding. She’d rather not be too self-aware about her image.
work: Sonic Youth’s Goo (1990) and “Kool Thing” put her on MTV in a cotton singlet, bootcut jeans, black choker. Experimental Jet Set, Trash and No Star (1994) and “Bull in the Heather” brought Kathleen Hanna into the video. The band’s downtown was also a fashion downtown: X-Girl launched 1993–94 with a guerrilla SoHo show two days after Cobain died.

Onstage later she has said she likes to dress against type and wear things that aren’t rock and roll, like a dress. The post-punk dress code was always t-shirts; when Mark Arm asked why she didn’t wear them anymore, she put on a giant T-shirt with nothing, just boots and a choker.

quotes.text: There’s a certain generic thing that happens with fashion that gives you confidence, like you’re fitting in. And I think there’s always been an element of me that wants to buck against that. I’ve always felt that’s why I’ve never really had such a great sense of style.
I was more mining Anita Pallenberg’s style, but also showing how clothes can change you into a different person.

The post-punk dress code was always t-shirts, and I remember Mark Arm from Mudhoney once asking me why I don’t wear t-shirts anymore. So I started wearing a giant T-shirt with nothing, just boots and a choker.

We wanted to do clothes that were fitted and casual. But fitted wasn’t meant to be ‘tight,’ even though sometimes the clothes came out that way. There’s this whole tendency with skater looks that everything needs to be over-sized, but we wanted to do stuff that was more fitted for girls.
quotes.said_to: Paper, An Oral History of X-Girl

why_the_look: She dresses against the generic thing that makes you feel safe, and against the rock-uniform she is supposed to wear.
beliefs: X-Girl visual language, per the Paper oral history: Joseph Szabo’s 1970s teen photographs; deadstock Army-Navy; the perfect 70s Levi’s 517 cord; “60s meets preppy”; A-line; the least-cool thing made cool. Daisy: it was about taking things that were not punk rock, not indie rock, not hip-hop — and making them that.

moments.title: X-Girl guerrilla show, Mercer Street
moments.garments: Primary-color ringer tees, skater jeans, A-line minis, baby barrettes. Kim seven months pregnant, in a down jacket, out of her own samples. Bed-sheet backdrop.
moments.designer_season: X-Girl, 1994. Not a numbered seasonal RTW show — a street show. Production: Sofia Coppola + Spike Jonze. Models included Chloë Sevigny.
moments.where_it_lives: Angela Hill / IDEA X-girl Show; Vogue. Timed to the exit of Marc Jacobs, two days after Cobain’s death.
moments.why_iconic: The anti-runway: a painted sheet, no VIP list, indie-rock as fashion.
